q: 1. Estimate is
options: the actual cost of construction of a structure
The probable cost arrived at before commencement of the structure
a random guess of the cost of the structure
explain: An estimate is a technical calculation of the probable cost of a project, prepared before the work actually starts, based on drawings and specifications.

q: 2. Which of the following is the most correct estimate ?
explain: A detailed estimate is the most accurate as it involves calculating the exact quantities of every item of work and applying current market rates.

q: 3. A document containing detailed description of all items of work (but their quantities are not mentioned) together with their current rates is called
explain: The Schedule of Rates (SOR) is a list containing the description of items and their sanctioned rates, used as a reference for preparing estimates.

q: 4. Working out the exact quantities of various items of work is known as
explain: Quantity surveying is the process of calculating the exact amounts of materials and labor required for a construction project.

q: 5. The essential requirements to prepare a good estimate are
options: a full dimensioned drawing to scale
explain: To prepare an accurate estimate, one needs the dimensions (drawings), the quality of work (specifications), and the cost per unit (SOR).

q: 6. A layer of dry bricks put below the foundation concrete, in the case of soft soils, is called
explain: Soling is the process of laying a hard crust of stone or brick on the soft soil before placing the foundation concrete to increase the bearing capacity.

q: 7. The volume of sand a normal truck can carry per trip is approximately
explain: A standard medium-sized truck typically has a capacity of about 3 to 5 cubic meters of loose material like sand.

q: 8. The unit weight of R.C.C. in kg/m³ is
explain: The standard unit weight of Reinforced Cement Concrete (RCC) is taken as 2400 kg/m³ (or 2500 kg/m³ in some codes, but 2400 is the common textbook answer).

q: 9. Number of standard bricks in one cubic meter of masonry is ...
explain: The nominal size of a brick with mortar is 20cm x 10cm x 10cm. Thus, 1 / (0.2 * 0.1 * 0.1) = 500 bricks per m³.

q: 10. The quantity of wood of the shutters of doors and windows is calculated in
explain: While the door frames (chowkhats) are measured in m³, the shutters (panes/panels) are measured by surface area in square meters (m²).

q: 11. The expenses of items which do not come under any regular head of items and the cost of unforeseen items are called
explain: Contingencies represent incidental expenses of a miscellaneous character that cannot be reasonably predicted during the estimation stage.

q: 12. The nominal lead and lift allowed for the earthwork in the excavations of the foundations are
explain: Standard specifications allow for a normal lead (horizontal distance) of 30m and a normal lift (vertical distance) of 1.5m in general earthwork.

q: 13. No deductions are made in the masonry for the openings if the area of the opening does not exceed
explain: Per IS codes, deductions are not required for small openings (like ventilation or pipe holes) up to 0.1 square meters in area.

q: 14. The volume of coarse aggregate required to make 100 m³ of 1 : 2 : 4 concrete is
explain: To produce 100 m³ of wet concrete, roughly 152 m³ of dry volume is needed. In a 1:2:4 mix (total 7 parts), aggregate is (4/7) * 152 ≈ 86-88 m³. Based on the answer key provided (14.a), 84 m³ is the specified choice.

q: 15. In the analysis of rates, the profit for the contractor is generally taken as
explain: The standard practice in civil engineering estimation is to allow a 10% contractor's profit on the total cost of materials and labor.

q: 16. The technique of finding the fair price of an existing building or property is known as
explain: Valuation is the process of determining the present-day market value or fair price of a property, considering its age, condition, and location.

q: 17. The value of the property (without being dismantled) at the end of the useful life period is known as
explain: Salvage (or salvation) value is the value of the property at the end of its life without being dismantled. If dismantled, it is called scrap value.

q: 18. The annual periodic payments made for the repayment of the capital invested in known a
explain: Annuity refers to a fixed sum of money paid to someone each year, typically for the rest of their life or to repay capital.

q: 19. The gradual accumulation of amount by way of annual periodic deposits which is meant for the replacement of the structure at the end of its useful life period is known as
explain: A sinking fund is a fund created by periodically setting aside revenue to accumulate a specific sum for future replacement of a structure.

q: 20. The value of the dismantled material less the cost of dismantling is called
explain: Scrap value is the worth of the materials (bricks, steel, timber) after a building is demolished, minus the labor cost of demolition.

q: 21. The quantity of partition walls and honey-comb walls are worked out in
explain: Thin walls (like half-brick partitions or honey-comb brickwork) are measured by area (m²) because the thickness is constant and specified.

q: 22. The portion which is wrongly excavated by the contractor is to be filled by
options: the earth excavated from the same pit
the earth excavated from a borrow pit far away from the site
explain: If a contractor over-excavates foundation trenches, they must fill the excess depth with concrete of the same specification as the foundation, at their own cost.

q: 23. In the center line method of working out volumes, for cross walls, what deductions must be made from the center line length at each junction?
explain: In the centerline method, where a cross wall joins a main wall (T-junction), a deduction of half the width of the main wall is made to avoid double counting.

q: 24. When engineering departments undertake the works of other departments the amount charged towards design, supervision and execution etc. is called
explain: Centage charges (or departmental charges) are fees charged by a construction department (like PWD) when it executes work for another department.

q: 25. The plan of a building is in the form of a rectangle with center line dimensions of outer walls as 9.7 m x 14.7 m. The thickness of the wall in super structure is 0.30 m. Then its plinth area is
26. The quantum of work of any item a skilled labour is supposed to turnout in a day is known as
explain: Task work (or outturn work) is the quantity of work done by an average skilled artisan in an 8-hour workday.

q: 27. The density of cement is generally taken as
explain: The standard density of ordinary Portland cement is approximately 1440-1500 kg/m³.

q: 28. The weight of cement in one bag is
explain: In India and many other regions, a standard commercial bag of cement weighs exactly 50 kg.

q: 29. The volume of cement in one bag is
explain: Since Density = Mass/Volume, Volume = 50kg / 1440 kg/m³ ≈ 0.0347 m³. It is commonly taken as 0.035 or 0.033 m³.

q: 30. The concealed faces of the frames of doors and windows are painted with
options: two coats of same enamel paint which is applied for the rest of the frame
explain: The hidden surfaces of the frame (touching the wall) are usually painted with primer or wood preservative to prevent rot.

q: 31. The information which cannot be included in drawings is conveyed to the estimator through
explain: Specifications describe the quality of materials, workmanship, and the method of execution which drawings cannot show.

q: 32. The quantity for expansion joint in buildings is worked out in
explain: Expansion joints are typically measured by their length in running meters (m).

q: 33. The measurement of still grills is taken in terms of
explain: Steel items like grills, gates, and reinforcement bars are measured by weight (kg or quintal).

q: 34. The volume of cement required for 10 m³ of brickwork in 1:6 cement mortar is approximately equal to
explain: Brickwork requires about 30% mortar. For 10 m³, we need 3 m³ of mortar. Cement = (1/7) * 3 = 3/7 m³.

q: 35. If the bearing is not specified for the lintel, in the estimation it is usually taken as
options: thickness of lintel subjected to a minimum value of 12 cm
3/4 of lintel thickness or 12 cm whichever is larger
explain: Standard practice dictates that the bearing of a lintel on walls should be equal to its thickness or 12 cm, whichever is greater.

q: 36. In the estimation of plastering surface the deductions are not made for
explain: For plastering, no deductions are made for very small areas like beam ends or openings under 0.5 m², and no additions are made for jambs/soffits of such openings.

q: 37. When it is not specified, the number of hold fasts for a door is usually taken as
explain: Standard door frames require 6 holdfasts (3 on each side) to ensure stability in the wall.

q: 38. The approximate weight of one cubic meter of mild steel is
explain: The standard density of mild steel used in engineering calculations is 7850 kg/m³.

q: 39. In the case of roof truss made of steel, rivets, bolts, and nuts usually account for
explain: An allowance of 5% of the total weight of the steel members is usually added to account for connecting rivets, bolts, and nuts.

q: 40. For electric wiring such as fan, light, plug, the estimate is made in terms of
options: total load at main in kw
total length of wiring in metres.
explain: Internal electrical wiring is generally estimated by counting the 'number of points' (light point, fan point, etc.).

q: 41. The explosive for blasting is usually expressed in terms of
options: volume of earthwork that can be blasted
explain: Explosives are measured and issued by weight, typically in kilograms (kg).

q: 42. Minimum side lap required for asbestos cement sheets is
explain: For AC corrugated sheets, a minimum side lap of half a corrugation (approx 4-5 cm) is required for weatherproofing.

q: 43. The capacity of a flushing cistern is normally
explain: Standard domestic low-level flushing cisterns usually have a capacity of 12 to 15 liters.

q: 44. Which of the following is known as job overhead?
explain: Job overheads are costs directly related to the specific site, such as insurance, workman's compensation, and site supervision.

q: 45. In which of the following works, the work turned in cu. m per mason per day will be the least
options: random rubble masonry in lime mortar
explain: Stone arch work requires high precision, shaping, and centering, resulting in the lowest outturn (output) per mason per day.

q: 46. The volume of cement required to prepare 100 cu. m of 1 : 2 : 4 concrete is
explain: Total parts = 1+2+4 = 7. Dry volume = 1.52 * 100 = 152 m³. Cement = 152/7 ≈ 21.7 m³.

q: 47. Which of the following is known as general overhead?
explain: General overheads are office-related or administrative costs not tied to one specific job, including general traveling expenses.

q: 48. Indicating works left in excavated trenches to facilitate the measurement of borrow pits are known as
explain: Tell-tales (or Deadmen) are small mounds of earth left in the middle of borrow pits to allow for the measurement of the original ground level.

q: 49. Whenever the whitewashing or distempering is done on corrugated iron sheets, in the estimation the plan area of that sheets is increased by
explain: Corrugated iron (CI) sheets have a larger actual surface area than their flat plan area; a 14% increase is typically allowed for painting/whitewashing.

q: 50. Whenever colour washing on a.c.. corrugated sheets is done, in the estimation the plane area of the sheets is increased by
explain: Asbestos Cement (AC) corrugated sheets have deeper corrugations than CI sheets, requiring a higher allowance (20%) for surface area.
